p: **Deniz Ateş,** 11. Lives in Bodrum, by the sea. Can hold her breath for two whole minutes. Has never told anyone that the sea talks to her.
**Can Yıldırım,** 11. Deniz's best friend. Builds drones out of old toasters. Has a joke for every situation, including the bad ones. (Can is pronounced like "John.")
**Mira Papadaki,** 12. A girl from Rhodes who collects old maps and does not like being told what to do. By anyone.
**Dede Halil.** Deniz's grandfather. A retired lighthouse keeper with a white beard, a very old boat and a lot of secrets.
**Baba (Kerem Ateş).** Deniz's dad. A diver who fixes boats. Worries a lot.
**Ophelia Marsh.** A billionaire collector of lost things. Owns three black yachts, two islands and no friends.
**The Salt Men.** Ophelia Marsh's divers. Black wetsuits. Silver masks. They never speak.

chapters.t: Chapter One: The Sea Knows My Name
p: Most kids in Bodrum think the sea is just water. Blue, salty, wet. Good for swimming in July, bad for swimming in January. Full of fish and tourists and jellyfish.
I know better.
The sea talks.

Not in words, exactly. Not most of the time. It's more like the way your mum sounds through the wall when you're nearly asleep. A murmur. A hum. A *shhhhh,* going in and out with the waves. But sometimes, when I put my head under the water and stay very still, the murmur turns into words.
*Hello, little one.*
*Mind the sea urchin by the red rock.*
*Your father's boat has a leak in the left side.*
(It did. Baba didn't believe me until it sank.)

My name is Deniz Ateş. I'm eleven. *Deniz* means "sea." My grandfather picked it. He said it was because on the night I was born, there was a storm, and the waves came all the way up the beach and knocked on the hospital door.
I thought he was joking. Dede Halil jokes a lot.
He wasn't.

I live in Bodrum, at the very bottom left corner of Turkey, where the land runs out and the sea begins. It's a white town. White houses with blue doors, climbing up the hills around a bay full of boats. There's a castle on a rock in the middle of the bay, built by knights five hundred years ago, with flags on the towers and peacocks in the gardens. There are windmills on the hill. There are ice cream shops and fish restaurants and men selling sponges from the backs of their boats. In summer, there are more tourists than people.
In November, it's quiet. Just us. And the sea.
On the day this story starts, I was underwater.

I was diving off the end of the old harbor wall, below the castle, where the water is deep and green and cold, and the bottom is covered in old stones from before the castle was built. Baba says I'm not allowed to dive there alone. I wasn't alone. My best friend Can was sitting on the wall above me, holding my towel and flying his newest drone, which he had built out of a broken hairdryer and four tiny propellers.
I was looking for octopuses. There's a big one that lives in a crack between two stones, and I'd named him Mehmet, and I visited him every day after school.
Mehmet wasn't home.
But something else was.
On the bottom, between the old stones, half-buried in the sand, something was shining. A little gleam of gold, catching the light coming down through the water.
I swam down. Deeper. My ears popped. The water got colder. I reached into the sand and pulled it out.
A coin. A tiny one, smaller than my fingernail. Gold. Very old. On one side, a face. A man with a beard. On the other side, a picture. A tower. A tall tower, on a rock, with a fire burning on top.
A lighthouse.
And the moment I touched it, the sea stopped murmuring.
It went completely quiet. All around me. As if the whole Aegean Sea was holding its breath.
And then it said, very clearly, in a voice like waves on a beach a long way off:
*Tideborn. At last. They are coming for the Library.*
I came up so fast that I hit my head on Can's drone.
"OW!"
"Hey!" Can grabbed the remote. The drone wobbled and spun and dived into the water next to me with a sad little *plop.* "Deniz! That was my best one! That was a Mark Seven!"
"Can," I said, treading water, holding the coin up out of the sea. "Can, the sea just talked to me."
Can looked at me. He looked at the bubbles where his drone had sunk. He looked back at me.
"Okay," he said. "Sure. And my drone just went to live with the fishes. It's a very weird day for both of us."

Can Yıldırım has been my best friend since we were three years old and he bit me at nursery school. (He says I bit him first. I didn't.) He is small and skinny, with huge glasses and hair that sticks up at the back no matter what his mum does to it. He wants to be an inventor. His room is full of broken toasters and radios and hairdryers that he takes apart and puts back together as robots, drones and, once, a machine that was supposed to make toast and accidentally set fire to the curtains.
He is also the only person in the world who knows that the sea talks to me.

Well. Knows is a big word. I told him when I was seven. He said "Cool." Then he asked if the sea could tell me where to find treasure. I said I didn't know. He said "Ask it next time." And that was that. He's never mentioned it since. Can is like that. He believes you, and then he gets on with things.
I climbed up the old stones onto the harbor wall, dripping, and sat down next to him and opened my hand.
The coin lay in my palm, gleaming. Wet and gold.
Can's eyes went huge behind his glasses.
"Is that *gold?*"
"I think so."
"Is that *real* gold? Like, *treasure* gold?"
"I think so."
He leaned so close that his glasses nearly touched it. "There's a tower on it. With a fire."
"A lighthouse," I said. "I think."
"And the sea talked to you. About it."
"It said *Tideborn.* And *at last.* And *they're coming for the Library.*"

Can sat back. He looked out across the bay. At the castle, and the boats, and the white town going up the hill. At the sea, flat and blue and calm, sparkling in the November sun, as if nothing at all had happened.

"Okay," he said slowly. "So. Three questions. One. What's a Tideborn? Two. What library? Three." He pointed at the bubbles where his drone had sunk. "Can you ask the sea to give me back my Mark Seven?"
I put my hand in the water at the bottom of the steps.
*Please,* I thought. *Just this once.*

A small wave came rolling up the steps. It splashed over my feet. And when it went back down, there, on the bottom step, dripping, with seaweed tangled in its propellers, was a drone made out of a hairdryer.
Can stared at it for a very long time.
"Okay," he said finally. "Okay. That's new."
My grandfather lives in a lighthouse.

Well. Next to one. The old lighthouse on the point at the end of the bay, on the rocks, where the land runs out. It's not a real lighthouse anymore. The government put up a new electric one, on a pole, ten years ago, and the old one was closed. But Dede Halil was its keeper for forty years, and when they closed it, he refused to leave. He lives in the little white keeper's house at the bottom of it, with three cats, two hundred books and a parrot called Pirate that only knows rude words.
We ran there. All the way along the beach, past the closed-up summer cafés, up the path over the rocks. I had the coin in my fist. Can had his wet drone under his arm.

Dede Halil was sitting outside his door, on a wooden chair, mending a fishing net, with his pipe in his mouth. He's very old. Older than anyone I know. He has a white beard like Father Christmas, and brown skin as wrinkled as a walnut, and blue eyes the color of the sea in the morning. He wears the same thing every day: a blue fisherman's jumper with holes in the elbows, and a captain's hat that he says he won in a card game in Marseille in 1963.
"Dede!" I shouted. "Dede, look!"
He looked up from his net.
He saw me running, dripping. He saw Can, behind me, with the drone. He saw my fist.
And something in his face changed. Something I had never seen before. He went very still. He took the pipe out of his mouth.
I skidded to a stop in front of him and opened my hand.
Dede Halil looked at the coin for a long, long time.
Then he looked up at me. And his blue eyes were wet.
"Where," he said quietly, "did you find that?"
"In the harbor. Under the castle. By Mehmet's rock."
"Mehmet?"
"The octopus."
"Ah." He nodded slowly, as if this made perfect sense. "And did the sea say anything? When you picked it up?"
I stared at him.
"How do you know about the sea?" I whispered.

My grandfather didn't answer. He put down his net, very carefully. He stood up. His knees cracked. He looked out at the bay, at the castle, at the long blue line of the sea going out to the horizon, toward Greece, toward Egypt, toward everywhere.
"It said *Tideborn,*" I said. "And *at last.* And *they're coming for the Library.*"
Dede Halil closed his eyes.
"So," he said, very softly, to the sea. "It's time."
Then he opened his eyes, and looked at me, and Can.
"Come inside," he said. "Both of you. Pirate, behave yourself. We have guests."
"*BARNACLE-BRAINED BILGE RAT!*" screamed Pirate from inside the house.
"That," said Dede Halil, "was him behaving himself."

chapters.t: Chapter Four: The Keepers of the Tide
p: Dede Halil's kitchen is small and crooked and smells of fish and pipe smoke and old paper. There are books everywhere. On the shelves, on the chairs, on the floor, in the oven. (He doesn't use the oven. He says ovens are for people who don't like fish raw enough.) There are maps on the walls. Old sea charts, brown and curling, with sea monsters drawn in the corners and coastlines that don't look quite right.
He made us tea. Then he sat down at the kitchen table, across from us, and put the coin in the middle of the table, on a white saucer, like something very precious.
"Two thousand three hundred years ago," he said, "in the city of Alexandria, in Egypt, there was a library."
"The Library of Alexandria," said Can immediately. "We did it at school. The biggest library in the ancient world. All the books in the world. And it burned down."

"That's what they teach you," said Dede Halil. "Yes. It had half a million scrolls. Every book that anyone had ever written, from Greece and Egypt and Persia and India and Babylon. Mathematics. Medicine. Astronomy. Poetry. History. Inventions. Maps of the stars and maps of the world. Everything humans knew." He tapped the coin. "And in the harbor of Alexandria, there was a lighthouse. The Pharos. The tallest building in the world, after the pyramids. With a fire on top that ships could see from fifty kilometers away. One of the Seven Wonders."
"That's the tower on the coin," I said.

"That's the tower on the coin," said Dede Halil. "Now. The library burned. That much is true. It burned many times, over hundreds of years. Julius Caesar burned part of it by accident. Then others burned more. Wars. Riots. Emperors who didn't like books. By the end, it was gone." He leaned forward. "But not all of it."
The kitchen was very quiet. Even Pirate.

"Before the last fire," said Dede Halil, "a group of people saved what they could. The librarians. The scholars. The keepers of the lighthouse. They loaded the most important scrolls onto ships, at night, in secret. Thousands of them. The best of everything. And they sailed out of the harbor, past the lighthouse, and away across the sea." He spread his old hands on the table. "And they hid them. Somewhere under the sea. Somewhere nobody could ever burn them. In a library built under the water."
"The Sunken Library," I whispered.

"The Sunken Library," said Dede Halil. "And they made a promise. They would keep its secret. They would pass it down, father to son, mother to daughter, keeper to keeper. They would never let anyone find it who would sell it, or burn it, or use it to make themselves rich and powerful. They would wait until the world was ready." He looked at me with his sea-blue eyes. "They called themselves the Keepers of the Tide."
"And you're one," said Can slowly. "Aren't you? You're a Keeper of the Tide."

"I'm the last one," said Dede Halil. "As far as I know." He picked up the coin and held it to the light. "And the Keepers had one more secret. Once in a hundred years, maybe less, a child is born who can hear the sea. Who can talk to it. Who can ask it for help, and sometimes, it helps." He put the coin in my hand and closed my fingers around it. "We call them Tideborn."
I looked at the coin in my fist. At my grandfather's old hands around mine.
"That's me," I said. "Isn't it?"
"The night you were born," said Dede Halil, "the waves came all the way up the beach and knocked on the hospital door." He smiled. "I told you I wasn't joking."
"So where is it?" said Can. "The Sunken Library. Where is it?"
Dede Halil laughed. A big, rumbling, beardy laugh that made Pirate fly off his perch.
"If I knew that, boy," he said, "do you think I'd be living in a lighthouse with a rude parrot?"

He got up and went to the wall. To the biggest of the old sea charts, brown and curling, pinned up over the kitchen sink. He took it down. Behind it, set into the wall, there was a little wooden door. A cupboard. With a keyhole shaped like a wave.
He took a key from a string around his neck, under his fisherman's jumper. He unlocked the cupboard.
Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, there was something flat and heavy. He brought it to the table and unwrapped it.

It was a sheet of bronze. Thin, about the size of a page in a school exercise book, green and brown with age, and covered in tiny engraved lines. Waves. Islands. Coastlines. Tiny ships. And writing. Greek letters, very small, very neat.
And one edge of it was straight. The other three were jagged. As if it had been cut, or broken, out of something bigger.

"The Lighthouse Map," said Dede Halil. "Or one piece of it. The Keepers engraved it on bronze, two thousand years ago, so that it would never burn, and never rot. A map to the Sunken Library. And then, so that no one person could ever find the Library alone, they cut it into five pieces. And hid each piece in a different place. At a wonder of the world." He laid his hand on the bronze. "This one has been in our family for nine hundred years. Passed from Keeper to Keeper. It shows the beginning of the route. From Alexandria, where the ships set out." He tapped a tiny engraving of a tower with a fire. "But the rest is missing. Four more pieces. Nobody has seen them all together for two thousand years."
"Five pieces," said Can. "Five wonders. Which wonders?"
"That is where your coin comes in," said Dede Halil.
He held out his hand. I gave him the coin. He turned it over and over in his fingers.

"The Keepers made five of these," he said. "Five gold coins. And they hid them, one near each piece of the map. Not with the pieces. Near them. Like a signpost. Like a key." He held the coin up to the window. "This one shows the lighthouse. The Pharos. But the coin was found here. In Bodrum. In our harbor. Under the castle." He looked at me. "So what wonder was in Bodrum?"

Can's hand shot up, like in school. "The Mausoleum! The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus! Bodrum used to be called Halicarnassus! There was a giant tomb for a king called Mausolos, and it was so big and so beautiful that it was one of the Seven Wonders, and that's why big tombs are called mausoleums now! We did it in fourth grade!"
Dede Halil looked at him with great respect. "You listen in school."
"Only to the interesting bits," said Can.

"The Mausoleum," said Dede Halil. "Yes. It stood on the hill above the harbor for sixteen hundred years. Then an earthquake knocked it down. And five hundred years ago, when the Knights of Saint John built the castle on the rock in the bay, they needed stones." He pointed out of the window. At the castle, with its flags and its towers, glowing gold in the afternoon sun. "So they took them. From the ruins of the Mausoleum. Thousands of them. Carved stones. Statues. Lions. They built the wonder of the world into the walls of their castle."
"So the first piece of the map," I said slowly, "is somewhere in the castle."
"Somewhere in the castle," said Dede Halil. "Or under it. Where you found the coin." He wrapped the bronze page back up in its oilcloth. "And now I must tell you why the sea said *they are coming.*"
He went to the window and pointed.
Out at the mouth of the bay, past the castle, past the windmills, a ship was coming in from the open sea.
A yacht. Huge. Long and sleek and pointed, like a knife. Painted completely black. Black hull. Black windows. Black sails, furled. Even the flag on the back was black.
It came gliding into Bodrum bay, slowly, silently, and stopped in the middle of the water, right in front of the castle. And dropped its anchor with a long, rattling splash.
"Her name is Ophelia Marsh," said Dede Halil.

We were standing at the kitchen window, all three of us, watching the black yacht. It sat in the middle of the bay like a shark in a goldfish bowl. Every fishing boat in the harbor had gone quiet. People on the waterfront had stopped to stare.

"She's English," said Dede Halil. "Or American. Or Swiss. Nobody is quite sure. She is one of the richest people in the world. She made her money buying and selling things. Oil. Gold. Companies. And then, when she had more money than she could ever spend, she started buying something else." He looked at me. "Lost things."
"Lost things?" said Can.

"Treasure from shipwrecks. Paintings that were stolen in wars and never found. Statues from temples. Ancient manuscripts. Things that should be in museums, where everyone can see them. She buys them, or finds them, or steals them, and she takes them to her islands, and nobody ever sees them again." His voice was hard. "She has a collection, they say, that would make the British Museum cry. Locked in vaults. Under the sea. Just for her. Just so she can own it."
"And she wants the Sunken Library," I said.

"Half a million scrolls," said Dede Halil. "Every lost book of the ancient world. The lost plays of Sophocles. The lost mathematics of Archimedes. The maps of Pytheas, who sailed to the edge of the world. Medicines nobody has seen for two thousand years. All the knowledge we lost." He looked out at the black yacht. "And she would lock it in a vault. And sell bits of it, maybe, to whoever paid most. A cure for a disease, for a billion dollars. A lost play, for the richest collector. Knowledge, for whoever can afford it."
"That's horrible," said Can.

"That's Ophelia Marsh," said Dede Halil. "She found one of the coins last year. In Rhodes. She's been looking for the rest ever since. And for the Keepers." He turned away from the window. "She found my name three months ago. She has written to me every week since. Very polite letters. Offering me money. A lot of money." He almost smiled. "I use them to light my pipe."
There was a knock at the door.
All three of us jumped. Pirate screamed something unrepeatable.
Dede Halil went very still. Then he went to the door and opened it.
A woman was standing on the step.

She was tall and thin and very elegant, in a long white coat and white gloves and a white hat with a wide brim. Everything about her was white, except her eyes, which were black. Very black. Like the windows of her yacht. She was older than Baba but younger than Dede, and she was smiling, with very white, very even teeth.

Behind her, on the path, stood two men in black wetsuits. Tall and silent, with their faces covered by silver masks. Smooth, blank, shiny masks, like mirrors, with two small dark holes for eyes. Water was still dripping off them.
"Mr. Halil Ateş," said the woman. Her voice was soft and pleasant and very slightly bored. "At last. I'm Ophelia Marsh. You haven't been answering my letters."
"I've been using them," said Dede Halil politely, "to light my pipe."
Ophelia Marsh laughed. It was a beautiful laugh. It didn't reach her eyes at all.
"How charming," she said. Then her black eyes moved past him. Into the kitchen. To me. To my hand. My closed fist, with the coin inside it.
"And who is this?" she said softly.
"My granddaughter," said Dede Halil. He moved so that he was standing between us. "And her friend. They were just leaving."

"Oh, please don't leave on my account." Ophelia Marsh stepped into the kitchen. Without being asked. She looked around at the books and the charts and the cats, with a little smile, the way you'd look at a funny old shop. She stopped in front of me and looked down. "What a pretty girl. What's your name, dear?"
I didn't say anything.
"Deniz," said Can. Then he looked horrified at himself. "Sorry. It just came out. I'm bad at secrets."

"Deniz," said Ophelia Marsh. "The sea. How appropriate." She crouched down, so her face was level with mine. Up close, she smelled of expensive perfume and seawater. "Have you been swimming today, Deniz? Your hair is wet."
"I swim every day," I said.

"In the harbor? Under the castle?" She smiled. "My divers found some very interesting things down there this morning. Old stones. Old carvings. And a little gap in the sand, where something had been dug up. Very recently." Her black eyes went down to my fist. "Something small. Something gold."
I put my hand behind my back.
Ophelia Marsh stood up. She turned to Dede Halil.

"Mr. Ateş," she said, "I'm going to make you an offer. One last time. And then I'm going to stop being polite." She took a folded piece of paper out of her white coat and put it on the kitchen table. "Ten million euros. For the bronze page in your cupboard. And the coin in your granddaughter's hand. And your help. Everything you know about the Keepers of the Tide." She smiled. "Ten million. Think what you could do. A new house. A new boat. A university education for your granddaughter. Anywhere in the world."
Dede Halil didn't even look at the paper.
"No," he said.
Ophelia Marsh sighed. A small, disappointed sigh, like a teacher whose student has got the answer wrong again.

"Mr. Ateş," she said. "You're a very old man, living in a very old house, protecting a very old secret that nobody cares about. Nobody. The world has forgotten the Library of Alexandria. They have phones now. They have the internet. Nobody will miss a few old scrolls." She picked up her piece of paper and put it back in her coat. "I'll find it anyway. With you or without you. I have three yachts, forty divers, a submarine, and all the time in the world." She turned to go. At the door, she stopped, and looked back at me. "You could have been very rich, Deniz. Remember that."
She walked out. The two Salt Men turned, without a word, and followed her, leaving wet footprints on the path.
Dede Halil closed the door.
Then he leaned against it, and let out a long breath, and I saw that his hands were shaking.
"Dede?" I said.
"She's right about one thing," said my grandfather quietly. "She'll find it. With or without us. She has a submarine." He looked at me. "Unless we find it first."
"Us?" said Can.
"Us," said Dede Halil. He looked at the coin in my hand. "Tonight. The castle."

chapters.t: Chapter Eight: The Lion in the Wall
p: Bodrum Castle closes at six o'clock. After that, the gates are locked, and there's a night guard called Ahmet Amca who sits in a little hut by the gate and watches football on a tiny TV and falls asleep by nine.
We didn't go in through the gate.
We went in from the sea.

Dede Halil's boat is called *Yakamoz.* That's a Turkish word that doesn't have a translation in English. It means the light that the sea makes at night, when tiny glowing creatures in the water sparkle when you move through them. *Yakamoz* is old and wooden and painted blue and white, with a little engine that coughs like an old man.

Dede Halil switched the engine off at the mouth of the harbor, and we rowed the rest of the way. Very quietly. In the dark. Past the black yacht, sitting silent in the middle of the bay with one light burning on its deck. Past the fishing boats. Around the back of the castle, where the walls go straight down into the sea.

At the bottom of the wall, just above the water, there were stones. Old, carved stones, built into the wall, different from the others. Bigger. Smoother. Covered in carvings worn soft by five hundred years of waves. A horse's leg. A piece of a chariot wheel. A man's face, half gone.
"The Mausoleum," whispered Dede Halil. "The Knights built it into the wall. Look for a lion."
It was so dark. The water slapped against the stones. I could barely see.
But I didn't need to see.
I put my hand in the water.
*Please,* I thought. *Where's the lion?*

The sea murmured. A wave came, very small, very gentle, and slapped against the wall about three meters to my left. And then another. And another. In exactly the same place. *Slap. Slap. Slap.* As if it was pointing.
"There," I whispered.

Dede Halil rowed us over. And there, half underwater, right at the waterline, was a lion. A stone lion's head, carved out of white marble, with a curly mane and a snarling mouth. Very old. Very worn. Water was going in and out of its mouth with every wave.
And on its forehead, between its stone eyes, there was a small round dent. The size of a coin.
I took out the gold coin. My hands were shaking. I pressed it into the dent.
It fit perfectly.
*Click.*
For a moment, nothing happened. The water slapped. The boat rocked. Somewhere in the bay, a dog barked.
Then the lion's mouth opened.

Not much. Just a crack. The stone jaw dropped down with a grinding sound, and the water rushed in, and kept rushing in. Pouring into the lion's mouth like water down a drain. Into some hollow space behind the wall.
"A sea cave," breathed Dede Halil. "Behind the wall. Under the castle." His eyes were shining in the dark. "Five hundred years, and nobody ever knew."
"How do we get in?" whispered Can. "The mouth's too small. And it's full of water."
I looked at the lion's mouth. At the black water pouring into it.
"I'll ask," I said.
I had never asked the sea for anything big before.

Small things, yes. Bring back a drone. Show me where the octopus is. Make a little wave splash in the right place. Small things, that the sea seemed happy to do, like a big friendly dog fetching a stick.
This was not a small thing.
I knelt at the edge of the boat. I put both hands in the water, up to my elbows. It was cold. November cold.
I closed my eyes.
*Please,* I said. *I need to get into the cave. Behind the lion. Please could you go out? Just for a little while? Just enough for us to get in?*
The sea didn't answer. It just murmured, the way it always did. *Shhhh. Shhhh.*
*Please,* I said again. *Somebody bad is coming. Somebody who wants to take the Library. The Keepers' Library. I'm a Tideborn. I'm trying to protect it.*
The murmuring stopped.
Everything stopped. The waves stopped slapping against the wall. The boat stopped rocking. The whole bay went flat and still and silent, like a mirror.
And then the sea *went out.*

Not the whole sea. Just around us. Just around the castle. The water drained away from the wall, slowly, smoothly, like a bath emptying, going down and down and down. The boat sank with it, gently, until it was sitting on wet stones and sand. And the lion's head rose up out of the water, dripping, with its stone mouth wide open. And below the lion, as the water went down, the wall kept going. Down and down. More carved stones. And at the bottom of them, at the very bottom, where the sea had covered it for five hundred years, there was an arch.
A low stone arch. A doorway. Into the dark.
Dripping. Waiting.
Can was holding on to the side of the boat with both hands, staring at me.
"You," he said. "Just. Moved. The *sea.*"
"I asked it," I said. My voice was shaking. My arms were shaking. "I just asked."
Dede Halil climbed out of the boat onto the wet stones. He had a flashlight. He shone it into the arch.
Stairs. Stone stairs, going down. Covered in seaweed and shells. Into the dark.
"The sea won't hold for long," he said. "It's doing you a favor. We should be quick."

chapters.t: Chapter Ten: The Room of the King
p: The stairs went down under the castle, under the rock, under the sea. Slippery and steep and cold. Seaweed hung from the ceiling and brushed our faces. Little crabs scuttled away from the flashlight. Water dripped everywhere.
And at the bottom, there was a room.

It was round. Small. Its walls were made of white marble, smooth and beautiful, not like the rough stones of the castle at all. Carved all around the walls, in a long line, there was a frieze. A carved picture, going all the way round. Soldiers. Horses. Chariots. Men fighting giant women with shields.
"Amazons," whispered Dede Halil. "That's the Mausoleum frieze. The Amazon battle. Some of it is in the British Museum in London. And some of it," he said softly, "is here."
In the middle of the room, there was a stone block. Like a table. Or a tomb. And on it, a statue. A man lying down, asleep, with a curly beard and a crown, and his hands folded on his chest.
"King Mausolos," I whispered.
And in his folded stone hands, he was holding something. Flat and green.
A bronze page.
I went to the statue. Slowly. My boots squelched on the wet stone. I reached out and touched the bronze.
And the sea, which had been murmuring very quietly the whole time, far away, behind the walls, said one word.
*Hurry.*
I pulled. The bronze page slid out of the stone king's hands. It was heavier than it looked. Covered in tiny lines. Waves and islands and ships.
"Got it!" I said.
And behind us, far away, up the stairs, I heard a sound. A rushing sound. A roaring sound.
The sea was coming back.
"RUN!" shouted Dede Halil.

We ran. Up the slippery stairs, with the flashlight swinging and the bronze page clutched against my chest. Can slipped and fell and Dede Halil hauled him up by his collar. The roaring got louder. Water was pouring down the stairs toward us now, ankle deep, knee deep, cold and fast, and we were running up into it.
We burst out through the arch at the bottom of the castle wall.
And the sea was right there. A wave. A big one. Coming back in, after holding its breath for too long.
The boat was on the stones, ten meters away.
"*Please!*" I screamed at the sea. "*Just one more second!*"
The wave stopped.
It *stopped.* In midair. A wall of black water, as tall as a house, curling over us, frozen, glittering in the light of Dede Halil's flashlight.
We ran. Across the wet stones. Into the boat. Dede Halil threw himself in last.
And the wave came down.

It came down gently. That's the thing. It could have smashed us to pieces. It came down like a hand putting a cup on a table. It lifted the *Yakamoz* up off the stones, and floated us out into the dark harbor, and set us down, rocking softly, on the calm black water.
And behind us, the lion's mouth closed, with a grinding of stone. And the arch vanished under the sea. As if it had never been there at all.
We sat in the boat in the dark, soaking wet, breathing hard.
Then Can started to laugh. Helplessly. Hysterically. Lying on his back in the bottom of the boat, in a puddle, laughing up at the stars.
"I'm going to need," he gasped, "a much better drone."
We didn't see them until they were already in the boat.

They came up out of the water, all around us. Silently. Three of them. Black wetsuits, silver masks, rising out of the sea like seals. Water pouring off them. One of them grabbed the side of the *Yakamoz* and the whole boat tipped. Another one reached for me. For the bronze page.
Can screamed.

Dede Halil grabbed an oar and swung it, and it hit a silver mask with a *clang* like a bell, and the Salt Man fell back into the water. But the other two were climbing in. Reaching. Their gloved hands were cold and wet and strong. One of them closed around my wrist.
I didn't think.
I threw myself over the side of the boat. Into the sea.
The water closed over my head. Black and cold and silent. The Salt Man let go of my wrist. I sank, with the bronze page held against my chest, down into the dark.
And the sea caught me.
*Tideborn,* it said. Not a murmur. A voice. Clear and deep and very, very old. *Hold your breath. Hold on.*
Something came out of the dark toward me. Big. Fast. I felt it before I saw it. A rush of water. A smooth gray shape. A fin.
A dolphin.

It came up under me, and I grabbed its fin without even thinking, the way you'd grab a hand in the dark. And we *went.* Fast. So fast. Through the black water, out across the harbor, away from the boat, away from the Salt Men, the water rushing past my face, my lungs burning, the bronze page under my arm, the dolphin's body warm and strong and alive under my hands.
Then up. Out. Into the air.

I gasped. The stars were spinning. The dolphin was swimming on the surface now, with me holding on, through the waves, across the bay. Behind us, I could see the *Yakamoz,* tiny and far away, with Dede Halil standing up in it, waving the oar, shouting. And two silver masks, bobbing in the water near it, turning their heads, looking for me.
They couldn't see me. Not in the dark. Not this far away.

The dolphin carried me all the way across the bay to the beach below the lighthouse, and slowed down in the shallow water, and stopped. I let go. I stood up, in the waves, up to my waist, shaking, with the bronze page in my arms.
The dolphin looked at me. With one dark, clever, friendly eye.
Then it blew a big spray of water out of its blowhole, right in my face, and laughed, the way dolphins do, *ek-ek-ek,* and turned and swam away into the dark.
I stood on the beach, soaking wet, and watched it go.
"Thank you," I whispered to the sea.
*You asked nicely,* said the sea. *Nobody asks nicely anymore.*
My dad found out the next morning.

Of course he did. Bodrum is a small town in November, and everyone knows everything. By breakfast, half the fishermen in the harbor were talking about how the sea had gone out around the castle in the middle of the night, all the way down to the sand, for nearly ten minutes, and then come back in again. The newspaper said it was "an unusual tidal event." The fishermen said it was a miracle. Old Hasan, who sells sponges, said it was the end of the world and closed his shop.

And Ahmet Amca, the night guard at the castle, said he had woken up from his football at midnight and looked out of his hut and seen a little blue and white boat sitting on the sand at the bottom of the castle wall. With an old man and two children in it.
Baba came up the path to the lighthouse at eight o'clock in the morning. Running.

My dad is big and strong and brown from the sun, with black curly hair and a black beard, and arms covered in scars from boat engines and fishing hooks and one shark (a small one; he says it was an accident; the shark says otherwise). He fixes boats for a living, and dives for a living, and he worries for a living. He has been worrying about me since the day I was born, and he is very, very good at it.
He burst into Dede Halil's kitchen. He looked at me. At my wet hair. At the bronze page on the table.
At his father.
"*What did you do?*" he said.
Dede Halil was making tea. He didn't turn around.
"Good morning, Kerem," he said. "Sit down. Have some tea."

"I don't want tea! Baba, what did you *do?* Ahmet says he saw you! On the sand! In the middle of the night! With *my daughter!*" His voice was shaking. "And there's a black yacht in the bay that the harbor master says belongs to some billionaire. And men in masks were diving all night. And my daughter is sitting here with wet hair at eight o'clock in the morning." He turned to me. "Deniz. What is going on?"
I looked at Dede Halil. He looked at me.
Then he nodded.
So I told him.
The coin. The sea. Tideborn. The Keepers of the Tide. The Sunken Library. Ophelia Marsh. The lion in the wall. The sea going out. The Salt Men. The dolphin.
Baba didn't say anything the whole time. He just stood there, in the middle of the kitchen, getting paler and paler.
When I finished, he sat down. Very suddenly. On a pile of books.
"The sea," he said. "The sea talks to you."
"Yes."
"And you can ask it to do things. And it does them."
"Sometimes. If I ask nicely."
Baba looked at his father.
"You knew," he said. "All this time. You knew she could do this."
"I hoped," said Dede Halil. "Since the night she was born. The waves on the hospital door. You remember."
"I thought you were *joking.*"
"I never joke about the sea," said Dede Halil.
Baba put his face in his hands. He sat there for a long time.
Then he lifted his head and looked at me. And his face was different. Still frightened. But something else, too.

"When you were four," he said slowly, "you fell off the end of the harbor wall. I wasn't watching. Two seconds. I turned around and you were gone. I dived in after you, and I couldn't find you. The water was so dark. I was down there for a minute, two minutes, I couldn't find you." His voice cracked. "And then a wave came. Out of nowhere. On a calm day. And it put you on the steps. Just put you there. Sitting on the steps. Laughing." He stared at me. "I never told anyone. I thought I was going mad."
I didn't remember. I was four.
But I believed him.

"Baba," I said. "Ophelia Marsh is going to find the Sunken Library. With a submarine. And she's going to lock it up forever and sell it. Unless we find it first." I swallowed. "We need to go to Ephesus. Today."
My father looked at me for a long, long time.
Then he stood up.
"Nobody," he said, "takes my daughter across the sea without me." He looked at his father. "We'll take the *Mavi.* She's faster. And she has a proper engine. Not like your old coffee grinder."
"The *Yakamoz* is a classic," said Dede Halil, offended.

"The *Yakamoz* is a museum piece," said Baba. He turned to Can, who was sitting very quietly in the corner, eating a biscuit and trying to be invisible. "And you. Does your mother know where you are?"
"She thinks I'm at a science camp," said Can. "I told her there's a science camp."
"Is there a science camp?"
"There is now," said Can.

The bronze page from the Mausoleum fit against Dede Halil's page perfectly. The jagged edges slotted together like two pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. A coastline joined up. A line of tiny ships continued across the join, sailing north from Alexandria, past islands, toward somewhere that was still missing.
And on the new page, in the corner, there was a picture.
Four women. Standing in a row. Each one in a little arched niche, like a window, with her hands folded. And underneath them, a line of Greek writing.
Dede Halil read it out slowly, with his finger under the letters.
"'Where Wisdom, Knowledge, Thought and Virtue stand guard, the sea once came to the door. Follow the sea that left.'"
§CLUE Where Wisdom, Knowledge, Thought and Virtue stand guard, the sea once came to the door. Follow the sea that left.
"Four statues," said Can. "Wisdom, Knowledge, Thought and Virtue." He was frowning. "Where have I seen that?"

"The Library of Celsus," said Baba suddenly. Everyone turned to look at him. He shrugged, a bit embarrassed. "I took a tourist boat to Kuşadası once, for the engines. They had a trip to Ephesus. There's a big library there, a Roman one, with the front still standing. And four statues of women in the front of it. The guide said they were Wisdom and Knowledge and..." He frowned. "Something. I was thinking about the engines."

"Sophia, Episteme, Ennoia and Arete," said Dede Halil. "Wisdom, Knowledge, Thought and Virtue. Yes. The Library of Celsus, in Ephesus. One of the greatest libraries in the ancient world, after Alexandria." He tapped the page. "And Ephesus had a wonder too. The Temple of Artemis. One of the Seven."
"But 'the sea once came to the door,'" I said. "Ephesus isn't by the sea. It's inland. We went on a school trip. It's miles from the sea."

"Five kilometers," said Dede Halil. "Now. But two thousand years ago, Ephesus was a port. One of the busiest in the world. Ships came right up to the city. The sea came almost to the library's door." He smiled. "And then the river brought mud down from the mountains. Year after year. Century after century. And the harbor filled up. And the sea went away. It left. It walked away from Ephesus, five kilometers, and never came back."
"Follow the sea that left," I said.
We sailed that afternoon.

The *Mavi* is my dad's boat. She's bigger than the *Yakamoz,* and faster, and painted dark blue, with a proper engine and a little cabin with two bunks and a kitchen the size of a cupboard. Baba uses her for diving trips with tourists in summer. In winter, he paints her and fixes her and talks to her when he thinks nobody can hear.
We went out of Bodrum bay, past the castle. Past the black yacht.
It was still there. Sitting in the middle of the bay. And as we went past, I saw a figure in white on its deck, holding a pair of binoculars.
Watching us go.

chapters.t: Chapter Fourteen: The Sea That Left
p: Ephesus is a city of ghosts.

That's what it feels like, walking through it. A whole Roman city, made of white marble, with streets and temples and fountains and houses and toilets (Can was very interested in the toilets) and a theater big enough for twenty-five thousand people. And nobody lives there. Nobody has lived there for a thousand years. It's just stones, and grass, and lizards, and the wind, and a few tourists.

It was nearly empty in November. Grey sky. Cold wind. A guide with an umbrella was walking a small group of Japanese tourists down the long marble street, and a cat was asleep on a broken column, and that was all.
We walked down the main street, the Curetes Street, which goes downhill between rows of broken columns and statues without heads. And at the bottom, there it was.
The Library of Celsus.

It's only the front. The rest fell down in an earthquake a thousand years ago. But the front is still standing, two stories tall, white marble, with columns and windows and carvings, glowing in the gray light. It's the most beautiful building I've ever seen. More beautiful than Bodrum Castle. It looks like a palace in a dream.
And on the front, in four arched niches, there are four statues. Four women, in long robes, standing very still.
Under each one, there's a name carved in Greek. *SOPHIA. EPISTEME. ENNOIA. ARETE.*
"Wisdom, Knowledge, Thought and Virtue," said Dede Halil softly. "Still standing guard. After eighteen hundred years."
"They're copies," said Can, reading a sign. "The real ones are in a museum in Vienna."
"Everything good ends up in a museum in Vienna or London," said Dede Halil darkly.
I stood in front of the library and listened.
But there was no sea here. Of course there wasn't. The sea had left a thousand years ago. Five kilometers away. There was only the wind, cold and dry, blowing dust across the marble.
"Follow the sea that left," I said. "But how can I follow it? It's not here. It's gone."
Then I had an idea.
I knelt down. I put my hands flat on the ground. Not on the marble. On the earth between the stones. The old, dry, brown earth.
And I listened. Not to the sea. To the ground.
And very, very far down, so faint that I could barely hear it, there was something. A murmur. A whisper. A *shhhhh.*
The sea.

Not the real sea. The memory of it. Soaked into the ground, the way water soaks into a sponge. The sea had been here, once, for hundreds of years. Lapping at the stones. Carrying ships. And when it left, it left a little bit of itself behind. Deep down. In the earth.

*Tideborn,* it whispered. So faint. So old. *I remember. I remember the ships. I remember the scholars, coming down the road with their scrolls. I remember where they hid it. Follow me. Follow me to where I used to be.*
I stood up.
"This way," I said.
I followed the ghost of the sea.

It led me away from the Library. Away from the tourists. Down a long, straight road, paved with marble, with broken columns on both sides. The Arcadian Way, the sign said. The Harbor Road. Two thousand years ago, it went from the theater straight down to the harbor, and it was the grandest street in Ephesus, lit at night with lamps, so that people could walk down to the ships.
Now it went down to a field.
A long, flat, marshy field, full of reeds and frogs and mud. With the remains of a gate at the end of it, half sunk into the ground. The old harbor gate. Where the ships used to tie up.
The sea's whisper got louder as I walked. Stronger. I could feel it under my feet. In the ground. In the stones.
"Deniz," said Baba, behind me, nervously. "We're not supposed to go past the fence."
"I know," I said, and climbed over it.

The ghost of the sea led me to the old harbor gate. Three stone arches, sunk into the mud, covered in moss. And under the middle arch, half buried, there was a stone. A big flat one, like a step. With a carving on it, almost worn away. A ship. A little ship, with a sail.
I knelt down and brushed the mud off it.
And in the middle of the sail, there was a small round dent. The size of a coin.
"We don't have another coin," said Can.
"No," I said. "But the sea does."
I put my hand on the stone. I closed my eyes. And I asked the ghost of the sea.
*Please. Where's the coin?*

The whisper went very quiet. Then, under my hand, very faintly, I felt the ground move. A little shiver. Like something shifting. And the mud at the edge of the stone bubbled. Just a little. Water came up out of it. Seawater. Salty. The first seawater in Ephesus for a thousand years. A little trickle. Then a little puddle.
And in the puddle, glinting, was a coin.
Gold. Tiny. On one side, a bearded face. On the other side, a woman, holding a scroll.
I picked it up. I pressed it into the dent in the ship's sail.
*Click.*
The stone slid sideways, grinding through the mud.
Underneath, there was a hollow. A small stone box, sealed with lead. And inside the box, wrapped in something that had once been cloth and was now just brown dust, there was a bronze page.
"Three," whispered Dede Halil. "That's three."
And behind us, from the sky, came a sound. A *thwump-thwump-thwump.* Loud. Getting louder.
A helicopter. Black. Coming in low over the ruins of Ephesus. With a white figure in the open door.
"RUN!" shouted Baba.

We ran. Back up the Harbor Road, with the bronze page in my arms, and the helicopter roaring overhead, so low that the wind from its blades flattened the grass and blew dust everywhere. The Japanese tourists were screaming and taking photos at the same time. The guide was waving her umbrella. The cat on the broken column had disappeared.

The helicopter swung around in front of us and landed. Right in the middle of the Harbor Road. Blocking it. The door opened, and Salt Men jumped out. Four of them. Silver masks, black wetsuits, even here, on land, miles from the sea. They looked so strange. Like fish that had walked out of the water.
We turned. The other way. Toward the theater.

The Great Theater of Ephesus is enormous. A huge half-circle of stone seats, cut into the side of a hill, going up and up and up, sixty rows of them, with a stage at the bottom. Twenty-five thousand people used to sit there and watch plays. And fights. And once, the guide had told us on the school trip, a riot, when the silversmiths of Ephesus got angry with Saint Paul.
We ran across the stage and up the seats. Up and up. Dede Halil was puffing. Baba was half carrying him. Can was in front, his little legs going like a clockwork toy.
The Salt Men came after us. Fast. Silent. They didn't puff. They didn't get tired.
Halfway up, Can stopped.
"Deniz!" he gasped. "Keep going! I've got an idea!"
"Can!"

He pulled his backpack off his shoulders and unzipped it. Inside, there was a drone. A new one. Made out of what looked like a vacuum cleaner and an old radio. The Mark Eight. He had built it on the boat on the way to Ephesus.
He threw it into the air. It wobbled. It buzzed. It flew.
And it started to *talk.*
Very loudly. Through the radio speaker, which Can had wired into it. In a voice that echoed off the stone seats of the theater, so loud that it filled the whole valley.
"*ATTENTION! ATTENTION! THIS IS THE TURKISH POLICE! THE THEATER IS SURROUNDED! PUT DOWN YOUR SILVER MASKS AND COME OUT WITH YOUR FLIPPERS UP!*"
It was Can's voice. Recorded. Made deeper with some kind of gadget. It sounded completely ridiculous.

But the Great Theater of Ephesus was built two thousand years ago, by the best engineers in the world, so that a man whispering on the stage could be heard by twenty-five thousand people in the back row. Every sound is made bigger. Louder. Everywhere at once.
The Salt Men stopped. They looked around. At the stone seats. At the sky. At the voice coming from everywhere.
"*SURROUNDED!*" boomed the drone. "*TOTALLY SURROUNDED! BY LOTS OF POLICE! WITH... UM... DOGS! BIG DOGS!*"
And in the distance, along the road, real sirens. Real ones. Somebody, the guide maybe, had called the actual police.
The Salt Men looked at each other.
Then they turned and ran back toward the helicopter.
Can sat down on a stone seat, two thousand years old, breathing hard, holding the remote control. The drone buzzed in circles above his head.
"Big dogs?" I said, coming back down to him.
"I panicked," said Can. "I'm an inventor. Not a writer."
We sailed for Rhodes that night.

Ophelia Marsh's helicopter had gone. The police had come, and asked a lot of questions, and Baba had told them that we were tourists who had been frightened by a film crew, and they had believed him, mostly. We had gone back to the *Mavi* in the dark, and cast off, and headed south.

The third bronze page fit against the other two. The coastline went on. The line of tiny ships went on, sailing past more islands. And in the corner of the new page, there was a picture of a giant. A huge man, standing with his legs apart, one foot on each side of a harbor, with ships sailing between his legs.

"The Colossus of Rhodes," said Dede Halil. "Another wonder. A bronze statue of the sun god, as tall as a building, standing at the entrance to the harbor of Rhodes. It fell down in an earthquake, fifty years after it was built. Nobody even knows exactly where it stood."
"But the Keepers knew," I said.
"The Keepers knew," said Dede Halil.

I couldn't sleep. I went up on deck. Baba was at the wheel, in the little light from the compass, steering by the stars. Dede Halil was asleep in one bunk, snoring. Can was asleep in the other, with his drone on his chest like a teddy bear.

The sea was calm and black and full of stars. Not just the stars in the sky. The stars in the water. *Yakamoz.* The little glowing creatures, sparkling in our wake, a long trail of green-blue light behind the boat, like a comet's tail.
I sat at the back of the boat, and trailed my hand in the water, and watched the sparks swirl around my fingers.
*You are tired, Tideborn,* said the sea.
"A bit," I said.

*You asked for a great deal yesterday. The castle. The wave. Today, the ghost of the old harbor. It takes something from you. Each time.* The sea was quiet for a moment. *Your grandfather's grandmother was Tideborn too. Did he tell you? She asked me to part the water once, in a storm, to save a ship full of people. I did. And she slept for three days afterward.*
"I didn't know that."

*There are many things you do not know,* said the sea. *That is good. It means there is much to learn.* A pause. *There is another, you know. Like you. Not of the sea. Of the wind. A boy. In Istanbul. The winds talk to him the way I talk to you. They tell me about him. They are very proud of him.*
I sat up. "Another one? Like me?"

*He set the winds free,* said the sea. *All seven of them. Last winter. The winds have been singing about it ever since. Every wind that comes across the water tells me another story.* The sea sounded almost amused. *The winds are terrible gossips.*
I looked up at the sky. At the stars. At the dark, empty horizon.
Somewhere out there, there was someone else. Someone who heard things that nobody else could hear.
It made me feel a little bit less alone.
Rhodes is a city inside a castle.

The old town is completely surrounded by walls. Huge, thick, golden stone walls, with towers and battlements and a moat, built by the same knights who built Bodrum Castle. Inside, there are narrow streets of cobblestones, and old stone houses with arches and balconies, and mosques and churches and fountains, and the Palace of the Grand Master, like something out of a fairy tale.

And there's a harbor. Mandraki. A little round harbor, with windmills along its wall. And at its entrance, on two stone columns, one on each side, two bronze deer. A stag and a doe. Facing each other across the water.
"This is where people think the Colossus stood," said Baba, tying up the *Mavi.* "One foot on each side. Where the deer are now."
"But it didn't," said a voice.
We all turned around.

A girl was sitting on the harbor wall, right next to our boat, with her legs dangling over the water. She was about twelve, with very long black hair in a single thick braid, and a sharp, clever face, and big gold earrings. She was wearing a leather jacket that was too big for her, and she had a notebook on her lap, full of drawings.
Maps. I could see them from the boat. The whole notebook was full of maps.

"It didn't stand here," she said again, in English, with a Greek accent. "That's what the tourists think. It couldn't have. It would have fallen into the sea. The harbor's too wide." She closed her notebook. "It stood on the hill. Over there. By the old temple of the sun god. Facing the sea. Everybody who knows anything knows that."
"And who are you?" said Baba.
The girl looked at him. Then at Dede Halil. Then at Can. Then at me.
Then at the bronze page, wrapped in oilcloth, under my arm. Just one corner of it was showing. Green. Engraved.
Her eyes went very wide.
"You're them," she said. "Aren't you? The Keepers."
Dede Halil went very still.
"How do you know that word?" he said.
The girl reached into her leather jacket. And took out something wrapped in a red silk scarf. She unwrapped it on her knee.
A bronze page.
Green and brown with age. Engraved with tiny waves and islands and ships. With three jagged edges.

"My name is Mira Papadaki," said the girl. "My great-great-great-grandmother was a Keeper of the Tide. This was hers. My grandmother gave it to me before she died." She looked at me with fierce dark eyes. "And yesterday, a woman in a white coat came to my house and offered my mother a million euros for it."
Mira wouldn't let go of her page.

We sat in the little cabin of the *Mavi,* all five of us, squashed around the tiny table, with the three bronze pages laid out in a row, fitted together. And Mira sat at the end, with her page held against her chest, wrapped in its red silk scarf, and looked at us like a cat looking at a dog.
"How do I know you're really Keepers?" she said. "How do I know you're not working for *her?*"
"Because we've got three pages," said Can. "And she's got none."
"That's what someone working for her would say."
"That's what someone *not* working for her would say too!"
"Exactly," said Mira. "So it proves nothing."
Can opened his mouth. Then closed it. "Okay," he said to me. "I like her. She's annoying."

Dede Halil leaned forward. He looked at Mira's page, at the edge of it, the bit that was showing out of the red silk. Then he said something. Not in Turkish. Not in English. In a language I had never heard before. Old and rolling and strange, like waves on a shingle beach.
Mira's face went white.
She answered him. In the same language. Haltingly. As if she was remembering it from a long time ago.
Dede Halil smiled.

"The old Keepers' words," he said to us. "Every Keeper learns them as a child. A greeting. *The tide goes out, the tide comes in, the sea remembers.* And the answer." He looked at Mira gently. "Your grandmother taught you."
Mira nodded. Her eyes were shining.

"She made me say it every night," she whispered. "Before bed. She said one day I'd meet someone who knew the other half." She looked down at the page in her lap. "She died last spring. I thought I was the only one left. I thought the whole thing was just a story she told me."
Then she unwrapped the red silk scarf and laid her page on the table.

It fit against the third page. Perfectly. The coastline went on, down past more islands, toward the south. Toward Egypt. And the line of tiny ships curved round, sailing back the way they'd come. Back toward the start. Toward a tower with a fire on it.
And in the corner, there was a picture. A tower. On a rock, at the mouth of a harbor. And under the sea, in front of the tower, tiny carvings. Fallen columns. Statues lying on their sides. A sphinx.

"Alexandria," said Dede Halil softly. "The Pharos. The lighthouse fell down in earthquakes, seven hundred years ago. Its stones fell into the sea. And they're still there. Under the water. Statues and columns and sphinxes, all lying on the bottom of the harbor."
There were Greek letters under the picture. Mira read them out. She could read ancient Greek, it turned out. Of course she could.
"'Where the light fell into the sea, the last page sleeps with the queen who never stopped watching.'"
§CLUE Where the light fell into the sea, the last page sleeps with the queen who never stopped watching.
"Four pages," said Can. "One more. In Alexandria. Under the sea." He looked around the table. "And then we have the whole map."
"And then she has the whole map," said Mira darkly. "If she catches us."
"She won't catch us," I said.
I should have known better than to say that out loud.
They took Can that night.

It was my fault. I keep telling myself it wasn't, but it was. We were in Rhodes Old Town, the three of us, Can and Mira and me, getting dinner. Baba and Dede Halil were on the boat, studying the map. We were only supposed to be gone twenty minutes. Can wanted souvlaki. Mira knew a place. Down a narrow cobbled street behind the Street of the Knights, with lanterns hanging from the arches and cats sleeping in doorways.
We were walking back, eating, laughing, Mira telling us about her school and Can telling her about his drones, when the street went quiet.
Too quiet. No cats. No music from the cafés. No footsteps.
And then they were there. Coming out of the doorways. Out of the arches. Silver masks, glinting in the lantern light.
Four of them. Five.
"Run!" I shouted.
We ran. Through the narrow streets. Under arches. Up steps. Mira knew the old town like the back of her hand. Left, right, through a courtyard, through a gate.
But Can is small. And Can doesn't run fast. And Can stopped, for one second, to pick up a dropped piece of souvlaki.
When I looked back, two Salt Men had him by the arms. Lifting him off his feet. His glasses were falling off. He was kicking.
"Go!" he shouted. "Deniz, go! Keep the pages! Don't..."
A gloved hand went over his mouth. And they were gone. Back into the arches. Into the dark.

Mira grabbed my arm and pulled. I didn't want to go. I wanted to run after them. But there were more Salt Men coming down the street, and Mira was stronger than she looked, and she pulled me through a door and up some stairs and out onto a roof and across three more roofs and down a drainpipe and into an alley.
And then we stopped. And I sat down on the cobblestones, and I couldn't breathe.
Mira crouched down next to me. Her face was white.
"They'll want a trade," she said. "That's what she does. She'll want the pages. For him."
I didn't answer. I was shaking.
An hour later, back on the *Mavi,* a message came. Not a phone call. A bottle. A glass bottle, floating in the harbor, bumping against the side of our boat. With a piece of white paper inside it.
Baba fished it out. He broke it open. He read it, and his face went gray, and he handed it to me.
The handwriting was elegant and sloping, in green ink.

*Dear Deniz. Your friend is quite safe, and having some very good hot chocolate. He talks a great deal. Bring me all four pages to the Acropolis of Lindos at sunrise, and you may have him back. Come alone. Ophelia.*
*P.S. I do hope you'll be sensible.*

Lindos is a white village on the east coast of Rhodes, an hour's drive from the old town. It sits on a hill above a perfect blue bay, and above the village, on a huge rock that rises straight out of the sea, there's an acropolis. An ancient temple, with white columns, at the very top of a cliff, with the sea a hundred meters below on three sides.
We drove there in a taxi before dawn, the five of us. Baba and Dede Halil and Mira and me. And a taxi driver who was Mira's cousin. (Everybody in Greece, it turns out, is somebody's cousin.)
"Come alone," the note had said.
"Absolutely not," Baba had said.

So we made a plan. A very bad plan. Baba and Dede Halil and Mira would wait at the bottom of the rock, by the path. I would go up alone. With the four pages in a bag. And I would give them to Ophelia Marsh. And get Can back.
Because there was nothing else to do. Because Can was my best friend. Because he bit me when we were three, and I bit him back, and we had been best friends ever since.
"Don't," said Mira, at the bottom of the path. "Deniz. If you give her the pages, she'll find the last one. In Alexandria. She'll have the whole map. She'll find the Library."
"I know," I said.
"Then don't!"
"Would you?" I said. "If it was your best friend?"
Mira looked at me for a long time.
Then she looked away.

I climbed the path. Up the steep white stone steps, carved into the rock, in the gray light before dawn. Past the old walls of a castle. Past the place where a ship was carved into the cliff, two thousand years ago. Up and up. The wind was cold. The sea was a long way below, gray and quiet.
At the top, by the temple, among the white columns, Ophelia Marsh was waiting.
In her long white coat. With her white hat. And a cup of coffee in her white-gloved hand.
Beside her, with a Salt Man holding each arm, was Can. With his glasses on crooked and chocolate on his face. He saw me and his whole face crumpled.
"Deniz, no," he said. "Don't. Don't give her them."

"Good morning, Deniz," said Ophelia Marsh. She sipped her coffee. "What a beautiful view. Don't you think? I come here every year. I always think, if I owned this, I would close it to the public. The tourists ruin it." She held out her other hand. "The pages, please."
I looked down. Over the edge of the cliff. At the sea, far below, gray and calm.
And at the black yacht, anchored in the little round bay at the bottom of the rock. With its black sails furled, and its one light burning.
*Tideborn,* said the sea. Very quietly. From a hundred meters below. *I am here.*
"The pages, Deniz," said Ophelia Marsh. Her voice was still pleasant. But her eyes weren't.
I held out the bag.
She reached for it.
And Can said, very loudly, "Mark Nine. *Go.*"
From the pocket of his trousers, a drone shot up into the air.

It was tiny. Smaller than my hand. Made out of what looked like an electric toothbrush and two bottle tops and a lot of tape. It buzzed straight up between the white columns, and hovered there, over our heads. And a little red light on its front started to blink.
"What," said Ophelia Marsh, "is that?"

"A camera," said Can. "And a radio. It's been recording everything since you took me. Everything you said on the yacht. About the helicopter. About Ephesus. About the vaults in your islands. About the statue you stole from the museum in Beirut." He grinned, a chocolatey, crooked grin. "And it's sending it. Right now. To my mum's email. And the Turkish police. And the Greek police. And a newspaper in London."
Ophelia Marsh went very still.
"It isn't," she said.
"It is," said Can. "You gave me a room with a computer in it. To keep me busy. You said I could play games." He shrugged. "I don't really like games."
For the first time since I had met her, Ophelia Marsh's face changed. The pleasant smile disappeared. Her black eyes went flat and cold.
"Get it," she said to the Salt Men.
They let go of Can. Both of them. And jumped for the drone.

It buzzed away. Out between the columns. Out over the edge of the cliff. Over the sea. And the two Salt Men ran after it, reaching for it, and stopped right at the edge, with the sea a hundred meters below.
And Can ran. Toward me.
Ophelia Marsh grabbed him. By the collar. Her white glove closed on his jumper.
And I did the only thing I could think of.
I didn't ask the sea for anything. Not this time. I just shouted. As loud as I could. Over the edge of the cliff. To the sea, a hundred meters below.
"*PLEASE!*"
And the sea answered.

Down in the little round bay, under the rock, the water rose. All of it. All at once. A great, smooth, green swell, rising up out of the bay like a giant taking a deep breath. Lifting the black yacht. Up. And up. And up. Higher than any wave should ever go. Until the yacht was riding on top of a hill of water, tilting, its anchor chain stretched tight, and the people on its deck were screaming and grabbing for the rails.
Ophelia Marsh turned around. She looked down at her yacht. At her beautiful black yacht, tipping on top of a mountain of sea.
She let go of Can.
Then the sea put the yacht down. Gently. Very gently. Like setting down a cup. The swell went flat. The bay went calm. The yacht rocked, and settled.
And Can was beside me, and I had his arm, and we were running, down the white stone steps, down the path, past the castle walls, past the ship carved into the cliff. And nobody followed us.
At the bottom of the rock, Baba caught us both in his arms, and held us so tightly that I couldn't breathe.
Up at the top, among the white columns, a figure in a white coat stood very still. Watching us go.
Then she turned around and walked away.
"Did you really send it?" I said to Can, when I could breathe. "To the police? To the newspaper?"
Can took off his glasses and wiped the chocolate off them with his jumper.
"I sent it to my mum," he said. "The internet on the yacht was terrible." He put his glasses back on. "But she doesn't know that."
Before we left Rhodes, Mira had to call her mother.
"She thinks I'm at my cousin's," said Mira. She was sitting on the edge of the *Mavi,* holding Baba's phone as if it might bite her. "In Lindos. Doing homework."
"Is there a cousin in Lindos?" asked Can.
"There's a cousin everywhere," said Mira. "This is Greece."

She dialed. She put the phone to her ear. She waited. And then her whole face changed, and she started talking very fast in Greek, so fast that I couldn't follow any of it, even the bits that sounded a little bit like Turkish.
The voice on the other end got louder. And louder. Mira held the phone away from her ear. We could all hear it. A woman's voice, shouting in Greek. It didn't need translating.
Mira listened for a long time. Then she said something very quietly. Then she held out the phone. To Dede Halil.
"She wants to talk to you," said Mira. "She says if you're really a Keeper, you'll know the words."
Dede Halil took the phone. He held it to his ear.
And he said the old words. The Keepers' greeting. In that strange, rolling, ancient language, like waves on a shingle beach. *The tide goes out, the tide comes in, the sea remembers.*
The shouting on the other end stopped.
There was a long silence.
Then a woman's voice, very quiet, said the answer. In the same language.
Dede Halil closed his eyes.

They talked for a long time. In Greek, and then in English, and then in the old language, and then in Greek again. Dede Halil walked up and down the deck, with the phone to his ear, nodding. Once, he laughed. Once, he wiped his eyes.
When he finally handed the phone back to Mira, his face was soft.

"Your mother," he said, "knew the words too. Your grandmother taught her. When she was a little girl. She told me she had forgotten them. That she thought they were just a bedtime story." He smiled. "She remembered them very quickly."
Mira took the phone. She listened. Her mother was talking quietly now. Not shouting. Mira's face went through about five different expressions. Then she said, "Nai, Mama. Nai. S'agapo." And hung up.
"What did she say?" I asked.
Mira looked at the phone in her hand for a long moment.

"She said," said Mira slowly, "that my grandmother would have been very proud. And that if I don't call her every single night, she will personally swim to Egypt and drag me home by my braid." She looked up, and her eyes were shining. "And she said to tell the Tideborn girl thank you. For finding me."
"I didn't find you," I said. "You found us. You were sitting on the harbor wall."

"I was sitting on the harbor wall for three weeks," said Mira. "Every day. Waiting. My grandmother told me before she died. She said, 'When the black ships come, the Keepers will come too. Wait for them by the deer.'" She shrugged. "So I waited."
Nobody said anything for a moment.
Then Can said, "Three weeks? On a wall? In November?"
"I had a very warm coat," said Mira.
"You're very weird," said Can, admiringly.
"Thank you," said Mira.
From Rhodes to Alexandria is six hundred kilometers of open sea.

The *Mavi* had never been that far. Baba had never been that far. He sat up all night before we left, checking the engine, checking the fuel, checking the radio, checking the weather on his phone and frowning at it.
"There's a storm coming," he said. "From the south. Two days from now. If we go today, we'll get to Alexandria just ahead of it." He looked at the phone again. "Maybe."
"And if we wait?" said Mira.

"Then Ophelia Marsh gets to Alexandria first," said Dede Halil. "With her three yachts and her submarine. And she doesn't need the map to find the last page. She has divers who can search the whole harbor."
So we went.

The first day was fine. Blue sky. Blue sea. Flying fish skipping across the waves in front of the boat, like silver birds. Mira sat in the front of the boat with her notebook, drawing maps of everything. Can sat in the back, building the Mark Ten out of a broken electric fan. Dede Halil slept in the cabin. Baba steered.
I sat with my hand in the water, talking to the sea.
On the second day, the storm came early.

It came out of the south like a wall. Black clouds. Lightning. A wind so strong it pushed the tops off the waves and turned them into spray. And the waves got bigger. And bigger. Until the *Mavi* was climbing up the side of each wave like a car going up a hill, and then hanging at the top, and then crashing down the other side, so hard that the whole boat shook and everything in the cabin fell off the shelves.

Baba was at the wheel, soaked, shouting. Dede Halil was holding on to the cabin door. Can was being sick over the side. Mira had her arms wrapped around the mast, with her eyes shut, and her lips moving. Praying, I think. In Greek.
I knelt at the back of the boat, with both hands in the wild water, and asked.
*Please. Please. Calm down.*
The sea didn't answer.

It wasn't the sea's fault. I understood that, after a while. The storm wasn't the sea. The storm was the wind. The wind was pushing the sea, whipping it up, making it angry. The sea was just doing what the wind told it to.
And I couldn't talk to the wind.
*I'm sorry, Tideborn,* said the sea, very faintly, through the roaring. *I cannot stop. The wind is too strong. I cannot stop.*

A wave came over the side of the boat. A big one. Green and white. It knocked me flat. It swept across the deck and knocked Can off his feet, and he slid toward the edge, toward the open sea, and Baba let go of the wheel and dived and grabbed his ankle.
The boat spun. Sideways to the waves. The worst way. The next wave would roll us over.
I saw it coming. Huge and black, with a white top, like a cliff.
And then, from the north, behind us, a different wind came.

Cold. Clean. Bright. Like a winter morning. Like the first breath of air when you open the window on a snowy day. It came down from the north across the sea, against the storm, and where it touched the waves, they *calmed.* Just a little. Just enough. The huge black wave in front of us lost its white top, and sank, and became just a big gray swell, that lifted the *Mavi* up, and set her down.
And the cold wind wrapped itself around the boat, like an arm around a shoulder. And I heard it.
Not the sea. The wind. For the first time in my life, I heard the wind talk.

*Hello, little Tideborn,* it said. *A friend of yours sent me. In Istanbul. A boy with a blue scarf. He heard about you from the sea. He says, hold on. He says, the winds are free now, and they help their friends.*
I stared up at the sky. At the black clouds, starting to tear apart. At a single star, shining through.
*He says,* said the North Wind, *that he is in Alexandria too. With his cousin and his friend. On holiday. He says, look for the boy whose breath is frosty.*

The storm didn't stop. But it got smaller. And smaller. The waves went down. The wind dropped. And by midnight, the *Mavi* was rocking gently on a long, slow, gray swell, under a sky full of stars, with all of us lying on the deck, soaked and exhausted and alive.
"What happened?" whispered Mira. "The storm just... changed."
"A friend," I said. "A friend of a friend."

Alexandria came out of the sea at dawn. A long, white city, curving around a huge bay, with tall buildings along the waterfront and palm trees and minarets and seagulls. Old trams rattling along the seafront road. Fishing boats painted every color. And at the end of the bay, on a rocky point, a fortress.
Square and pale and solid, with round towers at the corners and a flag on top.

"The Citadel of Qaitbay," said Dede Halil. He was standing at the front of the boat, holding on to the rail, with his white beard blowing. "Built five hundred years ago. On the exact spot where the Pharos stood. They used the lighthouse's own stones to build it." His voice was very quiet. "This is where it all began, Deniz. Two thousand years ago. This is where the Keepers loaded the scrolls onto the ships, at night, and sailed out past the lighthouse, and never came back."
We tied up in the old fishing harbor. And the first thing we saw, on the harbor wall, was a black yacht.
Not Ophelia Marsh's yacht. A different one. Her second one. Black, sleek, silent. With men in black wetsuits on its deck, checking diving equipment.
And on its deck, a crane. And hanging from the crane, a yellow submarine.
"She's here," said Mira. "Already."
"She doesn't have the map," said Can. "We have the map."

"She doesn't need the map," said Baba quietly. "She has forty divers and a submarine. She'll search every centimeter of that harbor." He looked at the fortress, and the water in front of it, gray-green and choppy. "We have to find it first. Today."
"The queen who never stopped watching," said Mira, reading from her notebook. "Under the water. Where the light fell into the sea."
"There are a lot of statues down there," said Dede Halil. "Hundreds. Sphinxes. Pharaohs. Queens. It's one of the biggest underwater ruins in the world."
And then a voice behind us said, in Turkish, "Excuse me. Are you the girl who talks to the sea?"

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Six: The Boy With the Frosty Breath
p: There were three of them, standing on the harbor wall, with an older man and an older woman behind them.
A boy about my age, thin, with messy dark hair and a blue scarf with little white flowers around his neck, even though it wasn't cold.
A girl a little older, with two long braids and glasses, holding a fat notebook held together with tape.
And a big boy, the biggest boy I'd ever seen, in a golden wrestling mask pushed up on his head like a hat, with a feather and a white hair stuck in the hatband, and red sneakers, eating a falafel.
The boy with the scarf breathed out. And his breath came out as a little cloud of frost. Sparkling. In the warm Egyptian air.
"I'm Kuzey," he said. "The wind told me about you. I hope that's okay."
I didn't know what to say. So I said, "The sea told me about you too."
Kuzey grinned. "The winds say the sea's a terrible gossip."
"The sea says the winds are worse."
We looked at each other for a long moment. And then we both started laughing, and couldn't stop.
Behind me, Can said, "Is anybody going to explain what's happening?"

"No," said the girl with the braids, and the girl with the braids and Mira looked at each other, and at each other's notebooks, and something passed between them that I didn't understand. "I'm Ela," said the girl with the braids. "Kuzey's cousin. Is that a map?"
"Four pages of one," said Mira, suspiciously.
"Can I see?"
"No."
"Fair," said Ela. "I wouldn't let me either."
Mira almost smiled.
The big boy came and sat down on the edge of the harbor wall next to Can and offered him half his falafel. "I'm Bora," he said. "You look like you've been seasick."
"Two days," said Can. "Two whole days."
"I get seasick too," said Bora. "And I'm afraid of heights. And the dark. I've done loads of adventures anyway." He thought about it. "Mostly with my eyes shut."
Can stared at him. Then took the falafel.

The older man was Kuzey's Uncle Tarık, a professor with wild hair, who shook Dede Halil's hand for a very long time and asked about seventeen questions about the Keepers of the Tide in about thirty seconds. The older woman was Dr. Amira, an Egyptologist from Cairo, who had brought them to Alexandria for the winter holidays to see the underwater ruins. She looked at me, and at the bronze pages in Mira's arms, and said, "Oh, *Nermin,*" under her breath, as if someone had told her a joke.
"Nermin?" said Dede Halil, sharply. "Nermin Aydın? From Istanbul?"
"My grandmother," said Kuzey.
Dede Halil sat down on a bollard. Very suddenly. He took off his captain's hat and held it in his hands.

"I met her," he said slowly. "Fifty years ago. In Marseille. In a card game. She won my hat." He looked at the hat. "And then she gave it back, and said, 'One day our grandchildren will meet, Halil. And they'll need each other.'" He shook his head. "I thought she was joking."
"She never jokes," said Kuzey. "About things like that."

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Biggest Room in the World
p: We couldn't dive until the afternoon, because Dr. Amira's permit started at two o'clock. So in the morning, all of us went to the library.
Not the old one. The new one.

The Bibliotheca Alexandrina stands on the seafront, a little way along the bay from the fortress. It's the strangest, most beautiful building I've ever seen. It looks like a giant disc. A huge, tilted circle of glass and metal, rising out of the ground at an angle, like the sun coming up out of the sea. And around it, there's a curved wall of gray granite, carved all over with letters. Thousands of them. In every alphabet in the world. Greek and Arabic and Chinese and Hindi and Hebrew and ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, and Turkish, and alphabets I had never seen before.
"They built it twenty years ago," said Dr. Amira. "As close as they could to where the old library stood. To say that the world remembers."

Inside, it was one enormous room. The biggest room in the world, Can said, and I believed him. The roof was the glass disc, tilted up above us, made of hundreds of little windows that let in the sunlight soft and blue. And under it, going down and down in huge wide steps, like a waterfall made of terraces, there were reading tables. Thousands of them. And shelves. And people. Students, mostly. Hundreds of them. Reading. Writing. Whispering. Asleep on their books.
We stood at the top of the steps and looked down at it all.
"It's free," said Ela. She was reading a sign. "Anyone can come in. Anyone at all."
"Good," said Mira fiercely.

Bora and Can wandered off together to look at a display of old printing presses.
