Bora had decided, overnight, that Can was his new favorite person, and Can had decided the same about Bora, and they had already invented a handshake that took about a minute to do. Ela and Mira went to the map collection. They hadn't stopped talking to each other since breakfast. In three languages. Mostly arguing.
That left me and Kuzey.
We sat on the edge of one of the huge terraces, with our legs dangling, looking down at all the people reading.
"Can I ask you something?" I said.
"Sure."
"What's it like? When the wind talks to you?"
Kuzey thought about it for a long time.

"It's not like it used to be," he said. "I used to have them inside me. Three winds. Living in my chest. Arguing at three in the morning." He smiled. "I set them free. Last winter. All seven. So now it's different. Now they just come and visit. When they want to. Like friends who drop in for tea." He breathed out, and his breath sparkled, very faintly. "The North Wind still comes every morning. It says hello. I say hello back. Sometimes it freezes my tea, as a joke."
"Do you miss it? Having them inside you?"

"Sometimes," said Kuzey honestly. "It was very powerful. I could make snowstorms. Fly. Talk to typhoons." He shrugged. "But it's better now. They're happier. And they still help, when I ask." He looked at me. "What about you? What's the sea like?"
I thought about it.

"Big," I said. "And old. And kind, mostly. And sad, sometimes, about all the things that have sunk in it." I looked up at the glass roof, at the blue light coming through. "It never forgets anything. Every ship. Every person who ever swam in it. Every drop of rain." I swallowed. "I'm scared, sometimes. That I'll ask it for something too big. And it'll say yes."
Kuzey nodded slowly. As if he knew exactly what I meant.

"My grandmother said something to me once," he said. "When it was all over. She said the important part isn't the power. It's the asking." He shrugged. "I think she meant, as long as you keep asking, and don't start telling, you'll be okay."
We sat there for a while, looking at the thousands of people reading.
"Hey," said Kuzey. "Deniz."
"Yes?"
"If your sea and my wind ever need to work together," he said. "Like, for something big. You know where to find me." He grinned. "Kadıköy. Fifth floor. There's always tea."
"Bodrum," I said. "The old lighthouse. There's always fish."
"Raw fish?"
"My grandfather says ovens are for people who don't like fish raw enough."
Kuzey laughed so loudly that half the library turned around to look at us, and a librarian at a desk far below put her finger to her lips.
We both went bright red and stopped.
But we were still smiling when Dr. Amira came to fetch us for the dive.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Queen Under the Water
p: We dived that afternoon. Me and Kuzey and Baba.

Baba had diving tanks on the *Mavi,* from his tourist trips. And Dr. Amira had a permit for the underwater site, from the Egyptian government. So we went out in the *Mavi,* to a place in the bay just in front of the Citadel of Qaitbay, with the black yacht watching us from the harbor, and its yellow submarine hanging from its crane.
"Remember," said Baba, checking my mask for the fifth time. "Stay close. Don't go deeper than eight meters. If anything goes wrong, come up. Slowly."
"I know, Baba."
"I know you know. I'm saying it anyway. It's my job." He looked at Kuzey. "Have you ever dived before?"
"No," said Kuzey. "But I flew once. Is it similar?"
Baba looked at him for a long time. Then he looked at me. Then he sighed and checked Kuzey's mask too.
We went down.

The water in Alexandria's harbor is green and cloudy. Not like Bodrum, where you can see twenty meters. Here, you can see maybe five. Little particles drift in the water, catching the light, like snow. And the bottom comes up out of the green gloom slowly, as you sink. First shadows. Then shapes.
Then stones.
Huge stones. Blocks of granite, as big as cars, lying in heaps on the sea floor, covered in weed and shells. Columns. Dozens of them, lying on their sides, broken. And among them, statues.

A sphinx. Lying on the sand, with its lion's paws stretched out, and its pharaoh's face looking up at us through the green water. Fish swimming around its head. Another sphinx, smaller, broken in half. A huge stone foot. A hand. A giant head of a pharaoh, as big as a car, lying on its side in the sand, with its eyes open, staring at nothing.
It was the most amazing and the most frightening thing I had ever seen.
The Pharos. The great lighthouse. The wonder of the world. Lying in pieces on the bottom of the sea.
I put my hand on a fallen column. And listened.

The sea here was old. So old. It remembered the lighthouse standing. It remembered the fire on top, burning every night for sixteen hundred years. It remembered the ships coming in, following the light. It remembered the earthquake, and the lighthouse falling, piece by piece, into the water, with a sound like the end of the world.
And it remembered the Keepers.
*Tideborn,* it whispered. *The queen. She is still watching. Look for the one who looks at the sea.*
I looked around. At all the statues. All the sphinxes and pharaohs, lying on their sides, looking at the sand, at the fish, at nothing.
And then I saw her.

A little apart from the others. Standing up. The only statue still standing. A woman. A queen, with a crown on her head shaped like a vulture's wings, and a long dress carved so finely that it looked like it was rippling. She was taller than Baba. She was standing on the sea floor, upright, among the fallen columns, with her head turned slightly.
Toward the open sea. Toward the north. The way the Keepers' ships had sailed.
The queen who never stopped watching.
Kuzey was next to me. He saw her too. He pointed. I nodded.
We swam to her. In her hands, which were folded in front of her, holding a stone scroll, there was a slot. A thin, straight slot.
I didn't have a coin.
But I didn't need one. I put my hand on the queen's stone hands. And I asked.
*Please.*
The queen's stone scroll slid open. Like a drawer. And inside it, there was a bronze page.
I took it. My heart was pounding so hard that I could hear it through the water.
And then I heard something else. A hum. Low and mechanical. Coming through the green water, getting louder.
A light. Yellow. Coming toward us out of the gloom.
The submarine.

It came out of the green water like a giant yellow fish. Round and fat, with a big glass bubble at the front and two mechanical arms folded under it, like a crab's claws. And inside the glass bubble, I could see a face.
White coat. White hat. Black eyes.
Ophelia Marsh. Smiling.
Behind the submarine, swimming fast, came the Salt Men. Six of them. Silver masks glinting in the yellow light.
Baba grabbed my arm and pointed up. *Go. Now.*
But the submarine was between us and the surface. And the Salt Men were spreading out around us. In a circle. Closing in.
The submarine's mechanical arms unfolded. Slowly. Reaching.
I held the bronze page against my chest.
And I asked the sea.
Not for a wave. Not for a dolphin. I asked for something I had never asked for before. I didn't even know if it was possible.
*Please,* I said. *Make it cloudy. As cloudy as you can.*
The sea went *mad.*

Sand rose up off the bottom. All of it. All at once. In a great, rolling, choking cloud. Every grain of sand on the floor of Alexandria harbor, lifted up and swirled around, until the green water turned brown, then black. I couldn't see anything. Not my hand in front of my face. Not the queen. Not Baba. Nothing.
But neither could they.
The submarine's yellow light was just a faint glow, somewhere in the murk. The Salt Men were gone. Just shadows. Lost.

And the sea pushed me. Gently. Up. Away from the submarine. Away from the light. Toward the surface. And I felt Kuzey's hand grab mine, and Baba's hand grab my other arm, and we were going up. Up and up, through the dark water.
We broke the surface twenty meters from the *Mavi.*
And the Salt Men broke the surface right behind us. Three of them. Fast. Swimming toward us.
"Kuzey!" I gasped. "The wind! Can you..."
Kuzey was already breathing in. A big breath. And he breathed out. Not at the Salt Men. Up. At the sky.
He didn't shout. He didn't command. He just said, in a perfectly ordinary voice, as if he was talking to a friend on the other side of the street, "Hey. Could you give us a hand? Please?"
And a wind came down out of the clear blue sky.

A big one. Cold and bright. It hit the water between us and the Salt Men, and it pushed. And the sea, which had been on our side all along, pushed with it. Wind and sea together. A wave rose up out of nowhere, a long rolling green wave, with the wind behind it, and it picked up the three Salt Men and carried them away across the harbor, spinning, all the way back to the black yacht, and dropped them in a heap on its deck.

Then the wave turned around, and came back, very gently, and lifted me and Kuzey and Baba, and put us down on the deck of the *Mavi,* next to Dede Halil and Can and Mira, who were all staring with their mouths open.
Kuzey sat up on the deck, dripping, and looked at me, and grinned.
"Teamwork," he said.
I held up the bronze page. The fifth one.
"Teamwork," I said.
We laid all five pages on the floor of Dr. Amira's hotel room that night, and fitted them together.

It took a while. Mira and Ela did it. They wouldn't let anyone else touch them. They knelt on the carpet side by side, turning the pages, sliding them, arguing in whispers, until the last jagged edge clicked into place.
And there it was.
The Lighthouse Map. Whole. For the first time in two thousand years.

It showed the eastern Mediterranean. Egypt at the bottom. Turkey at the top. Greece on the left. All the islands, scattered like seeds. And a line of tiny ships, sailing out of Alexandria, past the lighthouse, north across the sea. Stopping at Rhodes. At Ephesus. At Bodrum. And then turning west. Past Crete. Toward a tiny island, between Crete and the mainland of Greece. So small it was almost nothing. Just a dot.
And next to the dot, a drawing. A wheel. A bronze wheel, with teeth, like a gear in a clock. And under it, Greek letters.
"Antikythera," read Mira. Her voice was shaking.

"Antikythera," whispered Uncle Tarık. He had gone completely pale. "The Antikythera wreck. A Roman shipwreck, found by sponge divers in 1900. Full of treasure. Statues. Pottery. And a machine. A bronze machine, with gears, like a clock. Two thousand years old. The oldest computer in the world. It could predict eclipses and the movements of the planets. Nobody knew the ancient Greeks could build anything like it." He stared at the map. "Nobody has ever known why that ship was there. Or where it was going."
"It was going to the Library," I said.
Under the drawing of the gear, there was one more line of writing. Mira read it, very slowly.
"'The Library opens for the one who knows what a library is for.'"
§CLUE The Library opens for the one who knows what a library is for.
Everybody was quiet.
"What *is* a library for?" said Bora, eventually.
"Books," said Can.
"Keeping books safe," said Mira.
"Knowledge," said Ela.
"Reading," said Kuzey.

I didn't say anything. I was looking at the map. At the line of tiny ships. Sailing away from a burning library, two thousand years ago, carrying everything the world knew. To hide it. To keep it safe.
Until the world was ready.
"I don't know," I said. "Not yet."
Out of the window, in the harbor, the black yacht's lights were on. All of them. And it was moving. Out of the harbor. Heading north. Heading west.

"She saw the map," said Dede Halil quietly. "In the submarine. She saw it in your hand, Deniz, before the sand came. Just for a moment." He looked at the black yacht, getting smaller. "Maybe long enough."
Antikythera is a rock in the middle of the sea.

A small, steep, rocky island, between Crete and Greece, with almost no trees and almost no people. Twenty people live there, Mira said. And goats. And a lot of wind. The sea around it is deep and blue and wild, with strong currents, and in winter, nobody goes there at all.

We got there two days later. All of us. The *Mavi* with Baba and Dede Halil and Can and Mira and me. And a fishing boat that Dr. Amira hired in Alexandria, with Kuzey and Ela and Bora and Uncle Tarık in it, and a captain who said he had been sailing for forty years and had never seen a wind like the one that pushed his boat across the sea, all the way from Egypt, in one day and one night, without stopping.
Kuzey looked very innocent when he said that.
We found the black yacht already there. Anchored in the bay below the island's cliffs. Silent. Dark. With its submarine gone from its crane.
"She's already down there," said Baba.
I stood at the front of the *Mavi* and looked at the water.
It was very blue. Very deep. And very, very quiet.

*Tideborn,* said the sea. But not in the friendly voice. Not in the murmur. In a voice I had never heard before. Deep and slow and ancient, like a bell at the bottom of the ocean. *You have come. At last. The Library has been waiting.*
"Where is it?" I said.
*Below. Where the ship went down. Where the gear was lost. Go down, Tideborn. Go down alone.*
"Alone?" I said.
*The Library opens for one,* said the sea. *Only one. The one who knows what it is for.*
I turned around. Everyone was looking at me. Baba, with his face white. Dede Halil, with his hat in his hands. Can and Mira. And on the other boat, Kuzey, Ela and Bora, leaning over the rail.
"I have to go alone," I said.
"No," said Baba. "Absolutely not. No."
"Baba."
"Deniz, she's down there! With her submarine! With her Salt Men!"
"I know." I took his hands. His big, rough, scarred hands. "The sea won't let anything happen to me. It promised. When I was four. Remember? It put me on the steps."
My father looked at me for a long, long time.
Then he took off his diving watch and put it on my wrist.
"Thirty minutes," he said, in a voice that shook. "Then I come down after you. Library or no Library."
Across the water, on the other boat, Kuzey cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted, "Deniz! What's the answer? What's a library for?"
I looked at the deep blue water.
"I'll find out," I said.
And I dived.
I didn't need a tank. I didn't need a mask. The sea held me. It wrapped around me like a coat, and went into my lungs like air, and I breathed it. I don't know how. I just did. Tideborn.
I went down. And down. Past the blue. Into the dark blue. Into the black. Fifty meters. A hundred. The water got colder, and colder, and darker, and then, far below, there was light.
Green light. Glowing. Coming from the sea floor.
And between me and the light, there was something huge.
A turtle.

The biggest turtle in the world. Bigger than a boat. Bigger than a house. Its shell was covered in barnacles and coral and weed, like a little island. Its flippers were as long as the *Mavi.* Its head was as big as a car, wrinkled and ancient, with two dark eyes, wise and slow and sad.
It was lying across the entrance to a cave. A cave in the side of an underwater cliff. With the green light shining out of it.
It turned its huge head and looked at me.

*Tideborn,* it said. Its voice was so deep that I felt it in my bones. *I am the guardian. I have guarded this door for two thousand years. Since the Keepers' ship went down above me, carrying the last of the scrolls and the bronze gear.*
"Hello," I said. My voice was very small in the huge dark water.

*Another came before you,* said the turtle. *An hour ago. In a yellow machine. A woman in white.* Its dark eyes blinked slowly. *I asked her the question. She answered. The door opened.* The turtle was quiet for a moment. *She is inside now.*
My heart stopped.
"She answered right?" I said. "She knew what a library is for?"
*She said,* said the turtle slowly, *"A library is for keeping things. The most precious things in the world. Safe. Locked. Where no one can take them."*
"And the door opened for that?"

*It was not wrong,* said the turtle. *A library does keep things. That is a true answer. A small, true answer.* It looked at me. *The door opens for any true answer. But the Library itself, Tideborn, will only give its treasures to the right one.*
The turtle moved. Slowly. Its giant body shifted aside from the cave entrance, sending a cloud of sand drifting up into the green light.
*Go in,* it said. *Find her. Before the Library decides what to do with her.*
I swam into the cave. And the water ended.

That's the only way I can describe it. I swam through the entrance, and the water just stopped, like the edge of a bubble, and I fell through it, into air, and landed on a stone floor. Dry. Warm. In the light.
And I was in the Library.

It was enormous. A huge round room, carved out of the rock under the sea, with a domed ceiling so high that I couldn't see the top. And the dome was made of water. The sea, held up above my head like a glass ceiling, with fish swimming across it, and the green light shining down through it, rippling across everything.

And everywhere, from the floor to the edge of the dome, there were shelves. Stone shelves, carved into the walls, in rings, one above another, going up and up and up, with stone staircases spiraling between them.
And on every shelf, scrolls.

Thousands of them. Hundreds of thousands. Rolled up, in leather cases and bronze tubes and clay jars, each one with a little tag hanging from it. Every one of them perfect. Not burned. Not rotten. Not damp. Two thousand years, at the bottom of the sea, and every single one perfect.
The Library of Alexandria.
All the lost books of the ancient world.
I stood there with my mouth open, dripping, in the green light.
And then I heard a voice. Echoing around the huge round room.
"Isn't it *beautiful?*"

Ophelia Marsh was standing on the third ring of shelves. On a stone walkway, halfway up the wall, with an armful of scrolls. Her white coat was wet. Her white hat was gone. Her black hair was loose around her shoulders. And she was smiling. A real smile, this time. A child's smile. The smile of someone who has finally got what they wanted most in the whole world.

"The lost books of Aristotle," she said, holding one up. "The lost plays of Sophocles. A hundred and twenty-three of them. Only seven survived, Deniz. Seven. And here are all the rest." She held up another. "The mathematics of Archimedes. The maps of Eratosthenes. The medicine of Herophilus. Things nobody has known for two thousand years. Things that could change the world." She laughed. "And they're *mine.*"
"They're not yours," I said.
"I found them."
"You *followed* me."

"Details," said Ophelia Marsh. She started down the stone staircase. "My Salt Men are bringing the submarine around. We'll start loading in an hour. It'll take months, of course. Years, perhaps. But I have time." She reached the bottom and stood in front of me. "And then I'll put them somewhere very safe. Somewhere nobody will ever find them. And I'll read them. All of them. Every one." Her black eyes shone. "And I'll be the only person in the world who knows what they say."
And the Library began to shake.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Four: What a Library Is For
p: It started with a drip.
One drop of water, falling from the dome above us. Landing on the stone floor between me and Ophelia Marsh with a tiny *plip.*
Then another. Then ten. Then a hundred.
The dome of water above us was bending. Sagging. Like a ceiling about to fall.
Ophelia Marsh looked up. Her smile went away.
"What's happening?" she said sharply.

*The Library has heard her answer,* said the sea. In my head. Deep and sad. *She has told it what she wants. To lock it away. To keep it for herself. To be the only one.* A pause. *That is not what the Keepers saved it for. So the Library will close. Forever. And take her with it.*
"No," I said out loud. "No, wait. Please wait."

The water was pouring down now. Not drops. Streams. Splashing across the floor. Around our feet. Around our ankles. The scrolls on the lowest shelves were safe, somehow. The water flowed around them, never touching them. But it was rising. Fast.
Ophelia Marsh ran for the cave entrance. Through the water, holding her armful of scrolls. She reached the edge of the bubble, where the cave mouth was.
The sea pushed her back. Gently. Firmly. Like a door closing.
She turned around. Her face was white. "Let me out," she said. To me. "Deniz. Tell it to let me out."
The water was at my knees. At my waist.
I looked at her. At the scrolls in her arms. At her black eyes, frightened now. For the first time.
And I understood.
I understood what the Keepers had been waiting for. For two thousand years. What the world needed to be ready for.
"A library," I said, out loud, to the Library, to the sea, to the scrolls, to the turtle outside, to everyone, "isn't for keeping things."
The water stopped rising.

"It's not for hiding things. Or owning things. Or being the only one who knows." My voice was shaking. "A library is for *sharing.* That's what it's for. That's what it's always been for. It's a place where anybody can come in. Anybody. Rich or poor. From anywhere. And read anything. And learn anything. For free. Because knowledge isn't anybody's. It's everybody's." I swallowed. "The Keepers didn't save the scrolls to hide them forever. They saved them so that one day, they could give them back."
Silence.
The water stood still, around my waist, glittering in the green light.
Then, very slowly, it began to go down.
Back up into the dome. Like rain falling upward. Every drop. Until the floor was dry, and the dome was a smooth, rippling ceiling of sea again, with fish swimming across it.
*Yes,* said the sea. Its voice was soft. Proud. *Yes, Tideborn. That is the answer. That is the whole answer.*
Ophelia Marsh was standing at the cave entrance with her arms full of scrolls. Staring at me.
"Sharing," she said slowly. As if it was a word in a foreign language. As if she had never said it before in her whole life.
"Yes," I said.
She looked down at the scrolls in her arms for a long, long time.
Then she walked across the dry stone floor, and put them back on the shelf. One by one. Very carefully.

"I never had a library card," she said, very quietly, with her back to me. "When I was a girl. We were very poor. I wanted one so badly. The library in my town had a sign on the door. *Members only.* Five pounds a year. My mother couldn't pay." She put the last scroll on the shelf. "I used to stand outside and look through the window."
She turned around. Her face was wet. I don't know if it was the sea.
"Everything I've ever bought," said Ophelia Marsh, "I've bought so that nobody can ever put a sign on a door in front of me again."
I didn't know what to say.
So I didn't say anything. I just held out my hand.
After a long moment, she took it.

The sea let us out together. It carried us both up, through the cave mouth, past the great turtle, which watched us go with its wise old eyes. Up through the black, and the dark blue, and the blue, toward the light.
We broke the surface at exactly twenty-nine minutes and forty seconds, by Baba's watch. My father was standing on the back of the *Mavi* in his diving gear, with one foot already in the water.
He hauled me out and held me so tight that I thought my ribs would crack. He didn't say anything. He just held on.
Ophelia Marsh climbed onto the black yacht by herself. She didn't look back.
But two days later, a letter arrived at the lighthouse in Bodrum. On thick white paper, in green ink.
*Dear Deniz,*
*I have closed my vaults. All of them. Everything in them is going back to the museums it came from. It will take some time. There is a great deal of it.*
*I will not go back to Antikythera. Nobody will, from me. You have my word, which I'm told is not worth very much, but I'm hoping to improve that.*
*I have also bought the library in the town where I grew up. I have taken the sign off the door.*
*Yours,*
*Ophelia Marsh*

*P.S. Please tell your friend Can that his drone is very good. My technicians cannot work out how he made it. I would like to offer him a job when he is older. He will probably say no. Tell him I said that was the right answer.*
So what did we do with the Sunken Library?

We argued about it for a week. All of us. In Dede Halil's kitchen, with Pirate shouting rude words, and Mira and Ela on a video call from Rhodes and Istanbul, arguing with each other in three languages.
In the end, we made a choice. The new Keepers of the Tide. Me and Mira. With Dede Halil and Mira's mother and, unofficially, a girl called Ela Aydın, who said she was "a consultant."
The Library stays where it is. Safe, at the bottom of the sea, with the great turtle at the door.
But every year, on the night the Keepers' ships left Alexandria, one scroll comes up.

Just one. Chosen by the Library itself. Carried up by the sea. And given to the new Library of Alexandria, the beautiful glass and granite one on the waterfront, where anyone in the world can walk in, for free, and read it.
The first one came up last month.

A lost book of medicine. About a plant that grows in the mountains of Crete, that the ancient doctors used to treat fever. The scientists in Alexandria are testing it now. Dr. Amira says they are very, very excited.
The second one is coming up next November.
Nobody knows what it will be. Not even me.
That's the best part.
On the first day of spring, I went diving off the end of the old harbor wall, below the castle, where the water is deep and green and cold.

Can was sitting on the wall above me, flying the Mark Twelve, which can carry a sandwich. Mira was sitting next to him, on holiday from Rhodes, drawing a map of Bodrum harbor in her notebook, and telling him he was holding the remote wrong.
The sea was murmuring. The way it always does.
*Hello, little one.*
*Mind the sea urchin by the red rock.*
*Your grandfather is reading a letter from Istanbul, and laughing.*

(He was. It was from Grandma Nermin. She had heard all about Antikythera from Kuzey. She wanted us all to come to Kadıköy for tea. She said she would make börek. She said she still had his hat, actually, and he could have it back if he won it fair and square this time.)
I swam down. To the bottom. To the crack between two old stones, where the big octopus used to live.
Mehmet was home.
He was sitting in his crack, with his eight arms curled around him, looking at me with his strange, clever eyes. And in one of his arms, he was holding something. Something small and shiny.
A coin.
Gold. Tiny. On one side, a bearded face. On the other side, a picture I had never seen before. Not a lighthouse. Not a library.
A wheel. With seven spokes. Like a compass rose.
And the sea said, very softly, very clearly, in a voice like waves on a beach a long way off:
*Tideborn. Well done. Rest now.*
*But not for too long.*
§END The End.

**The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus.** A giant tomb for King Mausolos, built in Bodrum about 2,350 years ago. One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The Knights of Saint John really did use its stones to build Bodrum Castle, and pieces of its carvings, including the battle of the Amazons, are now in the British Museum.

**The Library of Celsus, Ephesus.** A real Roman library, built about 1,900 years ago. Its beautiful front is still standing, with four statues of Wisdom, Knowledge, Thought and Virtue. The real statues are in a museum in Vienna.
**The harbor of Ephesus.** Ephesus really was a great port. Mud from the river filled up the harbor over hundreds of years, and today the sea is about five kilometers away.
**The Great Theater of Ephesus.** Big enough for about 25,000 people, and built so that a voice on the stage can be heard in the back row.

**The Colossus of Rhodes.** A giant bronze statue of the sun god, one of the Seven Wonders. It fell in an earthquake about fifty years after it was built. Nobody knows exactly where it stood. The famous picture of it standing over the harbor is probably wrong.
**Lindos.** A real village on Rhodes with an acropolis on a cliff above the sea, and a ship carved into the rock.

**The Pharos of Alexandria.** The great lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders, about 100 meters tall. It fell in earthquakes about 700 years ago. The Citadel of Qaitbay was built on its site, and divers really have found statues, sphinxes and columns on the harbor floor.

**The Library of Alexandria.** The greatest library of the ancient world. It was damaged and destroyed over hundreds of years. A beautiful new library, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened on the waterfront in 2002.

**The Antikythera Mechanism.** A real bronze machine with gears, found in a Roman shipwreck near the island of Antikythera in 1901. It is about 2,000 years old and could predict eclipses and the movements of the planets. It's in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.
**Yakamoz.** A real Turkish word for the glow of tiny sea creatures in the water at night. There isn't one English word for it.
